evidence: Lucr. 1.426: locus ac spatium, quod ināne vocāmus
M-O s.v. space (space travel): ināne īnfīnītum, after Egger
terms.comment: The void of Democritus and Epicurus, in which the atoms move (Lucretius, Cicero). Egger calls outer space ināne īnfīnītum, and sends spacecraft in ināne īnfīnītum (Morgan–Owens s.v. launch).

evidence: M-O s.v. space (space travel), after Egger
terms.comment: Egger also writes ināne spatium cosmicum and spatium īnfīnītum (Morgan–Owens).

phrases.latin: in īnfīnītō inānī, in quō nihil nec summum nec īnfimum nec medium nec ultimum nec extrēmum sit
phrases.english: in an infinite void, in which there is no top or bottom, no middle, no end and no edge

phrases.latin: tum porrō locus ac spatium, quod ināne vocāmus, sī nūllum foret, haut usquam sita corpora possent esse
phrases.english: then again, if there were no room and space, which we call the void, bodies could not be anywhere at all

sources: Lewis & Short: inanis · Lewis & Short: spatium · Lewis & Short: cosmicus
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. space; launch (a spacecraft).
Cicero’s De finibus and Lucretius checked against the Perseus Latin texts (9 November 2026).
Traupman has no word for outer space.
